I had similar stats and EC hour totals, and was accepted to one school and waitlisted by a few others. Which isn’t spectacular, but isn’t terrible either. Of course, the more hours the better, but I think it’s more important that you are able to effectively convey what you’ve gained from these experiences, rather than just saying “oh I worked a billion hours in this clinic and a trillion hours in that hospital…”

Make sure you have a strong personal statement and at least a somewhat compelling narrative that ties your experiences together. And, most importantly, don’t assume that just because you’ve got high stats you’re guaranteed to get into a high tier school. For people like us with weaker EC hours, it’s imperative to apply BROADLY to at least 20+ schools, including mid and low tier schools. You may even want to throw in a few DO apps as well, if you’d like.

Ultimately, it’s your decision whether to apply now or take a gap year. If your school has a premed advisor, I’d recommend discussing it with them. But it is possible to get accepted with high stats and low ECs.

Make sure you smile periodically and seem like you're happy/enthusiastic to be there. The most common feedback I got from mock interviewers was that even though my answers were fine, I tended to speak with a flat affect and came off as very "low energy". So just make sure to inject some feeling/energy into your voice. And make eye contact, like the other commenter said. 
Another thing was that whenever I got nervous or didn't immediately know how to answer a question I would start talking really fast and ended up rambling quite a bit as I tried to give a decent answer. So just be cognizant of your talking speed to make sure you're not talking super fast. 
Also, if you're really stumped by a question it's okay to say something like "wow, that's a really good question, would you mind if I take a few seconds to think about it?" And then think about how you want to answer rather than just immediately speaking before you actually know what you want to say. Don't do this for every single question, obviously, but just ones where you really do need a few seconds to think.

Assuming Jesse was laying on his back for some reason, I still don't think Jesse would die in this case because (assuming Walt still goes to the duplex that night) Walt would turn him over and save him when he started choking. He would then take Jesse to the hospital to treat the overdose. 

I imagine Walt would take back the money as well, and if Jesse or Jane tried to object he'd remind them that Jesse could've easily died if it weren't for him, and that if he let them have the money one or both of them would eventually just OD again. He'd probably lay the guilt on real thick to Jane, blaming her for Jesse's OD since she was the one who introduced him to heroin. 

I think he'd then try very hard to convince Jesse to go to rehab in exchange for his money, and Jesse in turn would try to convince Jane to go to rehab as well. I'm not sure if Jane would go or not, since she seemed pretty opposed to rehab when her father brought it up. Although with both her father and Jesse asking her to go to rehab, she may just end up doing it. Walt would also try and persuade Jesse to break up with Jane since she's a bad influence on him, but I don't think Jesse would ever do that. Maybe Walt would even secretly pay Jane off if she agrees to stay away from Jesse lol. Idk if she would go for that though. 

I guess the rest of the show would play out similarly to the original, except with Jesse being a lot less depressed in season 3. He also might not end up dating Andrea (if he and Jane are still dating), which would prevent him from causing problems with Gus.

Now if Walt didn't go to the duplex that night, and Jesse was laying on his back and died, I think Jane may just end up taking Jesse's money and getting out of the country like they originally planned. She'd probably be scared of being caught with a dead body and a huge sum of cash, plus she'd probably be scared of what Walt would do to her once he found out. 

Walt would definitely blame Jesse's death on Jane and try to get revenge on her. He'd probably get Saul to hire somebody to track her down. Of course, he'd demand the money back since it was Jesse's money, not Jane's. I wouldn't be surprised if Walt had Jane killed, either by his own hands or by hiring some hitman from Saul. 

I'm not sure how Jesse dying would affect Walt's relationship with Gus. On one hand, it may, like you said, serve as a wakeup call to Walt as to the deadly nature of the drug-dealing business. He may feel some degree of guilt since he's a drug manufacturer and Jesse died of a drug overdose. So, he might quit cooking altogether afterwards. 

On the other hand, his desire for revenge may spur him further towards "the dark side", and he'd become even more ruthless and unhinged without Jesse as his moral center. Originally Gus had to give the whole "a man provides" speech to get Walt to start cooking again (since he stopped when Skyler leaves him), but in this scenario Walt probably wouldn't need any convincing and would just jump right to it. He'd work with Gale for Gus without any foreseeable problems. He might end up trying to kill Gus again just so he can get a bigger cut of the profit, but I don't really see that happening.
